steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks an oxygen atom on the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 2′ carbon.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself to form stems and loops.

4. Location and roles  
   • DNA resides mostly in the cell nucleus (in eukaryotes) and stores genetic information long-term.  
   • RNA is found throughout the cell (nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria) and has multiple roles:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA) carries instructions from DNA to the ribosome.  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA) is a structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – Other RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, etc.) regulate gene expression.

5. Stability  
   • DNA’s lack of the 2′-OH group makes it chemically more stable—suitable for long-term information storage.  
   • RNA’s 2′-OH makes it more prone to hydrolysis, fitting its roles in transient information transfer and regulation.

In summary, DNA is the stable, double-stranded genetic blueprint built on deoxyribose and thymine, whereas RNA is a more versatile, single-stranded molecule built on ribose and uracil, serving in various stages of gene expression.
